recentItems.title: Everything you need to know about bird flu - Benjamin Anderson
recentItems.description:
Dig into the science of avian influenza to find out what makes the H5N1 virus so dangerous, and its potential to jump to humans.

--

While avian influenza used to infect mostly birds, in the past few years, it’s been found in over 70 mammal species, including cats, dairy cows, foxes, seals, and bears. Each new mammalian infection gives the virus more chances to drift or shift, spill over into humans, and ignite a pandemic. So, what is it about H5N1 that makes it so frighteningly flexible? Benjamin Anderson investigates.

Lesson by Benjamin Anderson, directed by Anton Bogaty.

recentItems.title: Why do some people have a better sense of direction than others? - Oliver Baumann
recentItems.description:
Dig into the neuroscience behind our sense of direction and find out why some people are better at navigating than others.

--

Whether you identify as a wayfinding whiz or get lost returning from the grocery store, your brain has a built-in navigation system that facilitates spatial skills, from sensing which direction is north to map-reading and route-learning. So, why do we still struggle to find our way? And why do some of us find ourselves lost more often than others? Oliver Baumann digs into our sense of direction.

Lesson by Oliver Baumann, directed by Anton Bogaty.

recentItems.title: Ever walk into a room and forget what you were doing? - Gabriel Radvansky
recentItems.description:
Dig into the phenomenon known as the doorway effect, where walking into a new space can make you forget what you were doing.

--

You enter your living room, then pause. Uh-oh, what was it that you were doing? You feel your mission’s momentum wane, and its aim is suddenly lost. So, what just happened? Well, you’re not alone; this is a common memory lapse phenomenon scientists have termed the “doorway effect.” Gabriel Radvansky explores why walking into a new space can make you suddenly forget what you were doing.

Lesson by Gabriel Radvansky, directed by Biljana Labović.

recentItems.title: What are tariffs, and how do they work?
recentItems.description:
Explore how tariffs work and dig into how their enactment can set off an economic chain reaction that impacts global trade.

--

In 1930, in hopes of supporting farms and manufacturing, President Hoover made a bold decision: he approved a sweeping 20% tax on all imported agricultural and industrial goods. But the plan completely backfired, leading exports to fall and global trade to decline. And it wouldn't be the last time a world leader was shocked by a tariff’s consequences. Trace the economic chain reaction of tariffs.

Directed by Avi Ofer.

recentItems.title: Plato’s infamous Ship of State thought experiment - Michael Vazquez
recentItems.description:
Dig into Plato’s infamous Ship of State thought experiment, which explores how democratic societies handle leadership and power.

--

Imagine a ship struggling in an endless storm. Its captain, though strong and commanding, is a terrible navigator. Neither he nor his crew have been trained to sail, yet they tirelessly vie for control through bribery, flattery, and mutiny, and ignore those with real navigation knowledge. This dysfunctional vessel is Plato's Ship of State. Michael Vazquez explores the infamous thought experiment.

Lesson by Michael Vazquez, directed by Luis Torres, Mr. Flama.

This video was produced in collaboration with the Parr Center for Ethics, housed within the renowned Philosophy Department at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. The Parr Center is committed to integrating abstract work in ethical theory with the informed discussion of practical ethical issues, and prides itself on the development of innovative and inclusive approaches to moral and civic education.

recentItems.title: The tragedy of Cassandra, the princess who predicted the fall of Troy - Iseult Gillespie
recentItems.description:
Dig into the Greek tragedy of Cassandra, who received the gift of prophecy but was cursed by Apollo to never be believed.

--

As a young woman, Cassandra of Troy had been pursued by the god Apollo, who offered her the gift of prophecy. But when she withdrew from his advances, he twisted his gift into a maddening hex: from that day on, Cassandra would be able to precisely see and describe the future— but her prophecies would never be believed. Iseult Gillespie details the Greek tragedy of the cursed seer.

Lesson by Iseult Gillespie, directed by Yael Reisfeld.

recentItems.description:
Learn more at https://brilliant.org/TedEd

To coincide with the 1964 Tokyo Olympics, Japan launched a groundbreaking bullet train that inspired countries around the world to invest in high-speed rail. Ning Zhao details the possibilities and hurdles facing high-speed rail transit.

recentItems.title: The magical forest realm hiding at the bottom of the ocean - Luka Seamus Wright and Salomé Buglass
recentItems.description:
Discover the ocean’s hidden kelp forests, and explore how these light-dependent organisms evolved to survive at dark depths.

--

Like any other plant, kelps require light to grow. Yet kelps found nearly 90 meters below the ocean's surface, where sometimes only 0.1% of sunlight can reach, grow as large as, and often even larger than, their shallow counterparts. So how have these large, light-dependent organisms adapted to thrive at such depths? Luka Seamus Wright and Salomé Buglass explore the ocean's hidden forests.

Lesson by Luka Seamus Wright and Salomé Buglass, directed by Upamanyu Bhattacharyya, Otter Studios.
